title: De Officiis
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
source: Translated by Claude from phi0474.phi055.perseus-lat1, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Et id quidem nemini video Graecorum adhuc contigisse, ut idem utroque in genere elaboraret sequereturque et illud forense dicendi et hoc quietum disputandi genus, nisi forte Demetrius Phalereus in hoc numero haberi potest, disputator subtilis, orator parum vehemens, dulcis tamen, ut Theophrasti discipulum possis agnoscere. Nos autem quantum in utroque profecerimus, aliorum sit iudicium, utrumque certe secuti sumus.
passages.english: And indeed I see that this has so far fallen to none of the Greeks, that the same man should work hard in both kinds and pursue both that forensic kind of speaking and this quiet kind of philosophical discussion, unless perhaps Demetrius of Phalerum can be counted in this number: a subtle debater, an orator not very forceful, yet pleasant, so that you can recognise the pupil of Theophrastus. As for me, how far I have advanced in each, let that be for others to judge; certainly I have pursued both.

passages.original: Formam quidem ipsam, Marce fili, et tamquam faciem honesti vides, quae si oculis cerneretur, mirabiles amores, ut ait Plato, excitaret sapientiae. Sed omne, quod est honestum, id quattuor partium oritur ex aliqua: aut enim in perspicientia veri sollertiaque versatur aut in hominum societate tuenda tribuendoque suum cuique et rerum contractarum fide aut in animi excelsi atque invicti magnitudine ac robore aut in omnium, quae fiunt quaeque dicuntur, ordine et modo, in quo inest modestia et temperantia.
passages.english: You see, Marcus my son, the very form and, as it were, the face of the honourable, which, if it could be seen with the eyes, would arouse, as Plato says, a wondrous love of wisdom. But everything that is honourable arises from one of four parts: for it is concerned either with the perception of truth and with ingenuity; or with preserving human society, giving to each his own, and good faith in contracts; or with the greatness and strength of a lofty and unconquered spirit; or with order and measure in all that is done and said, in which lie moderation and self-control.

passages.original: Maxime autem adducuntur plerique, ut eos iustitiae capiat oblivio, cum in imperiorum, honorum, gloriae cupiditatem inciderunt. Quod enim est apud Ennium: Núlla sancta sócietas Néc fides regni ést. id latius patet. Nam quicquid eius modi est, in quo non possint plures excellere, in eo fit plerumque tanta contentio, ut difficillimum sit servare sanctam societatem.
passages.english: But most people are led to forget justice above all when they have fallen into a desire for military commands, offices, and glory. For what we find in Ennius, "There is no sacred fellowship, nor faith, in kingship," applies more widely. For whenever something is of such a kind that several cannot excel in it, there usually arises such rivalry that it is extremely difficult to preserve the sacred fellowship.

passages.original: nam aut inimicitias aut laborem aut sumptus suscipere nolunt aut etiam neglegentia, pigritia, inertia aut suis studiis quibusdam occupationibusve sic impediuntur, ut eos, quos tutari debeant, desertos esse patiantur. Itaque videndum est, ne non satis sit id, quod apud Platonem est in philosophos dictum, quod in veri investigatione versentur quodque ea, quae plerique vehementer expetant, de quibus inter se digladiari soleant, contemnant et pro nihilo putent, propterea iustos esse.
passages.english: for either they are unwilling to take on enmities, or toil, or expense; or else through negligence, laziness, or inertia, or because they are so hampered by certain pursuits or occupations of their own, they allow those whom they ought to protect to be abandoned. And so we must consider whether what Plato says of philosophers may not be sufficient: that because they are engaged in the search for truth, and because they despise and count as nothing those things which most people eagerly seek and over which they usually fight one another to the death, they are therefore just.
passages.notes: The sense is 'whether it is not enough', i.e. Cicero doubts that this suffices; 'ne non satis sit' is rendered literally.

passages.original: Popilius imperator tenebat provinciam, in cuius exercitu Catonis filius tiro militabat. Cum autem Popilio videretur unam dimittere legionem, Catonis quoque filium, qui in eadem legione militabat, dimisit. Sed cum amore pugnandi in exercitu remansisset, Cato ad Popilium scripsit, ut, si eum patitur in exercitu remanere, secundo eum obliget militiae sacramento, quia priore amisso iure cum hostibus pugnare non poterat.Adeo summa erat observatio in bello movendo.
passages.english: Popilius as general was holding a province, and in his army Cato's son was serving as a recruit. When Popilius decided to discharge one legion, he also discharged Cato's son, who was serving in that same legion. But when, out of love of fighting, he had stayed on in the army, Cato wrote to Popilius that, if he allowed him to remain in the army, he should bind him with a second military oath, since, the former [oath] having lapsed, he could not lawfully fight with the enemy. So scrupulous was the observance in waging war.

passages.original: Nihil autem est amabilius nec copulatius quam morum similitudo bonorum; in quibus enim eadem studia sunt, eaedem voluntates, in iis fit ut aeque quisque altero delectetur ac se ipso, efficiturque id, quod Pythagoras vult in amicitia, ut unus fiat ex pluribus.
passages.english: Nothing, moreover, is more lovable or more binding than similarity of good character; for in those who have the same pursuits and the same wishes, it comes about that each takes as much delight in the other as in himself, and the result is what Pythagoras wants in friendship, that one is made out of many.

passages.original: Praeclarum igitur illud Platonis: Non, inquit, solum scientia, quae est remota ab iustitia, calliditas potius quam sapientia est appellanda, verum etiam animus paratus ad periculum, si sua cupiditate, non utilitate communi impellitur, audaciae potius nomen habeat quam fortitudinis.
passages.english: Splendid, therefore, is that saying of Plato: "Not only," he says, "should knowledge that is divorced from justice be called cunning rather than wisdom, but also a spirit ready to face danger, if it is driven by its own desire and not by the common good, should have the name of recklessness rather than of courage."

passages.original: Sed illud odiosum est, quod in hac elatione et magnitudine animi facillime pertinacia et nimia cupiditas principatus innascitur. Ut enim apud Platonem est, omnem morem Lacedaemoniorum inflammatum esse cupiditate vincendi, sic, ut quisque animi magnitudine maxime excellet, ita maxime vult princeps omnium vel potius solus esse. Difficile autem est, cum praestare omnibus concupieris, servare aequitatem, quae est iustitiae maxime propria.
passages.english: But this is the hateful thing: that in this elevation and greatness of spirit, obstinacy and an excessive desire for supremacy very readily spring up. For just as Plato says that the whole character of the Spartans was inflamed with the desire to win, so, the more anyone excels in greatness of spirit, the more he wants to be first of all, or rather to be alone. But it is difficult, when you have set your heart on surpassing everyone, to preserve fairness, which is the most proper quality of justice.

passages.original: Quanto Q. Maximus melius! de quo Ennius: Unus homo nobis cunctando restituit rem.Noenum rumores ponebat ante salutem.Ergo postque magisque viri nunc gloria claret.
passages.english: How much better Quintus Maximus [acted]! Of him Ennius [says]: "One man by delaying restored the state for us. He did not put rumours before safety. Therefore the man's glory now shines afterwards and all the more."
passages.notes: "Noenum" is an archaic form of "non". The line "postque magisque" is variously understood ("more and more hereafter").

passages.original: Atque etiam in rebus prosperis et ad voluntatem nostram fluentibus superbiam magnopere, fastidium arrogantiamque fugiamus. Nam ut adversas res, sic secundas immoderate ferre levitatis est, praeclaraque est aequabilitas in omni vita et idem semper vultus eademque frons, ut de Socrate itemque de C. Laelio accepimus. Philippum quidem, Macedonum regem, rebus gestis et gloria superatum a filio, facilitate et humanitate video superiorem fuisse; itaque alter semper magnus, alter saepe turpissimus;
passages.english: And also in prosperity, when things flow according to our wishes, let us take great care to avoid pride, disdain, and arrogance. For just as it is a mark of shallowness to bear adversity without moderation, so it is with prosperity; and admirable is evenness of temper throughout one's whole life, and always the same expression and the same countenance, as we have heard of Socrates and likewise of Gaius Laelius. Philip, king of the Macedonians, though surpassed by his son in achievements and glory, I see was his superior in affability and humanity; and so the one was always great, the other often most disgraceful;

passages.original: Nam quodHerculem Prodicus dicit, ut est apud Xenophontem, cum primum pubesceret, quod tempus a natura ad deligendum, quam quisque viam vivendi sit ingressurus, datum est, exisse in solitudinem atque ibi sedentem diu secum multumque dubitasse, cum duas cerneret vias, unam Voluptatis, alteram Virtutis, utram ingredi melius esset, hoc Herculi Iovis satu edito potuit fortasse contingere, nobis non item, qui imitamur, quos cuique visum est, atque ad eorum studia institutaque impellimur;
passages.english: For as to what Prodicus says of Hercules, as it appears in Xenophon, that when he was first coming to manhood, the time given by nature for choosing which way of life each person will enter on, he went out into a solitary place and, sitting there, long and greatly debated with himself, since he saw two ways, one of Pleasure, the other of Virtue, which it was better to take: this could perhaps happen to Hercules, born of the seed of Jupiter, but not likewise to us, who imitate whomever each of us has seen fit to, and are driven towards their pursuits and practices;
passages.notes: 'quodHerculem' is a scanning error for 'quod Herculem'.

passages.original: turpe enimn valdeque vitiosum in re severa convivio digna aut delicatum aliquem inferre sermonem. Bene Pericles, cum haberet collegam in praetura Sophoclem poëtam iique de communi officio convenissent et casu formosus puer praeteriret dixissetque Sophocles: O puerum pulchrum, Pericle!At enim praetorem, Sophocle, decet non solum manus, sed etiam oculos abstinentes habere. Atqui hoc idem Sophocles si in athletarum probatione dixisset, iusta reprehensione caruisset.
passages.english: for it is disgraceful and very faulty to bring into a serious matter talk fit for a banquet, or some frivolous talk. Pericles [spoke] well when he had the poet Sophocles as his colleague in the generalship, and they had met about their common duty, and by chance a handsome boy passed by and Sophocles had said, "What a beautiful boy, Pericles!": "But a general, Sophocles, ought to keep not only his hands but also his eyes under restraint." And yet if Sophocles had said this same thing at an inspection of athletes, he would have escaped just reproach.
passages.notes: 'praetura' is Cicero's Latin for the Athenian office of strategos (general). 'enimn' read as 'enim'.

passages.original: nec vero est quicquam turpius vanitate. Opificesque omnes in sordida arte versantur; nec enim quicquam ingenuum habere potest officina. Minimeque artes eae probandae, quae ministrae sunt voluptatum: Cetárii, lanií, coqui, fartóres, piscatóres, ut ait Terentius; adde hue, si placet, unguentarios, saltatores totumque ludum talarium.
passages.english: and indeed nothing is more disgraceful than falsehood. And all craftsmen are engaged in a mean trade; for a workshop can have nothing befitting a free man. And least of all are those trades to be approved which serve pleasures: "fishmongers, butchers, cooks, poulterers, fishermen," as Terence says; add to these, if you like, perfumers, dancers, and the whole *ludus talarius* [variety show].
passages.notes: 'hue' read as 'huc'. The 'ludus talarius' was a kind of low stage entertainment; its exact nature is uncertain.

passages.original: Omnium autem rerum nec aptius est quicquam ad opes tuendas ac tenendas quam diligi nec alienius quam timeri. Praeclare enim Ennius: Quém metuunt, odérunt; quem quisque ódit, periisse éxpetit. Multorum autem odiis nullas opes posse obsistere, si antea fuit ignotum, nuper est cognitum. Nec vero huius tyranni solum, quem armis oppressa pertulit civitas ac paret cum maxime mortuo, interitus declarat, quantum odium hominum valeat ad pestem, sed reliquorum similes exitus tyrannorum, quorum haud fere quisquam talem interitum effugit;
passages.english: Of all things, nothing is better suited to protecting and holding on to power than to be loved, and nothing more foreign to it than to be feared. For Ennius [puts it] admirably: "Whom they fear, they hate; whom each man hates, he wishes dead." And that no power can withstand the hatred of many, if it was unknown before, has recently been learned. Nor is it only the death of this tyrant, whom the state, oppressed by arms, endured and whom it obeys even now, when he is dead, that shows how much the hatred of men avails for destruction, but also the similar ends of other tyrants, of whom scarcely any escaped such a death;

passages.original: Nam qui eorum cuipiam, qui una latrocinantur, furatur aliquid aut eripit, is sibi ne in latrocinio quidem relinquit locum, ille autem, qui archipirata dicitur, nisi aequabiliter praedam dispertiat, aut interficiatur a sociis aut relinquatur; quin etiam leges latronum esse dicuntur, quibus pareant, quas observent. Itaque propter aequabilem praedae partitionem et Bardulis Illyrius latro, de quo est apud Theopompum, magnas opes habuit et multo maiores Viriathus Lusitanus; cui quidem etiam exercitus nostri imperatoresque cesserunt; quem C. Laelius, is qui Sapiens usurpatur, praetor fregit et comminuit ferocitatemque eius ita repressit, ut facile bellum reliquis traderet.
passages.english: For whoever steals something from, or seizes something from, any of those who rob together with him leaves himself no place even in a band of robbers; and the one called the pirate chief, unless he divides the plunder fairly, is either killed by his comrades or abandoned; indeed, robbers are even said to have laws which they obey and observe. And so, because of his fair division of plunder, Bardulis, the Illyrian brigand mentioned in Theopompus, had great wealth, and Viriathus the Lusitanian much greater; to him even our armies and generals gave way; but Gaius Laelius, the one who is called the Wise, when praetor broke and crushed him and so checked his ferocity that he left his successors an easy war.

passages.original: Mihi quidem non apud Medos solum, ut ait Herodotus, sed etiam apud maiores nostros iustitiae fruendae causa videntur olim bene morati reges constituti. Nam cum premeretur inops multitudo ab iis, qui maiores opes habebant, ad unum aliquem confugiebant virtute praestantem;
passages.english: To me, at least, it seems that not only among the Medes, as Herodotus says, but also among our ancestors, kings of good character were once established for the sake of enjoying justice. For when the needy multitude was oppressed by those who had greater resources, they used to take refuge with some one man outstanding in virtue;

passages.original: quidem Crassus, cum esset admodum adulescens, non aliunde mutuatus est, sed sibi ipse peperit maximam laudem ex illa accusatione nobili et gloriosa, et, qua aetate qui exercentur, laude affici solent, ut de Demosthene accepimus, ea aetate L. Crassus ostendit id se in foro optime iam facere, quod etiam tum poterat domi cum laude meditari.
passages.english: Lucius Crassus, indeed, when he was still quite a young man, did not borrow [his reputation] from elsewhere, but won for himself the greatest praise from that famous and glorious prosecution; and at the age at which those who are in training are usually rewarded with praise, as we have heard of Demosthenes, at that age Lucius Crassus showed that he was already doing excellently in the forum what even then he could have practised at home with credit.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence: 'Nam L.' in the preceding context belongs with 'Crassus'.

passages.original: In iis tamen, qui se adiuvari volent, non ne affligantur, sed ut altiorem gradum ascendant, restricti omnino esse nullo modo debemus, sed in deligendis idoneis iudicium et diligentiam adhibere. Nam praeclare Ennius: Bene fácta male locáta male facta árbitror.
passages.english: With regard to those, however, who wish to be helped not so as not to be ruined, but so as to climb to a higher rank, we ought by no means to be wholly tight-fisted, but should apply judgement and care in choosing suitable people. For Ennius [says] admirably: "Good deeds badly placed I consider bad deeds."

passages.original: est enim, ut mihi quidem videtur, valde decorum patere domus hominum illustrium hospitibus illustribus, idque etiam rei publicae est ornamento, homines externos hoc liberalitatis genere in urbe nostra non egere. Est autem etiam vehementer utile iis, qui honeste posse multum volunt, per hospites apud externos populos valere opibus et gratia. Theophrastus quidem scribit Cimonem Athenis etiam in suos curiales Laciadas hospitalem fuisse; ita enim instituisse et vilicis imperavisse, ut omnia praeberentur, quicumque Laciades in villam suam devertisset.
passages.english: For it is, at least as it seems to me, highly fitting that the houses of distinguished men should be open to distinguished guests, and it is also an ornament to the state that foreigners should not lack this kind of generosity in our city. It is also extremely useful to those who wish to have great power honourably to be strong in resources and influence among foreign peoples through their guests. Theophrastus indeed writes that Cimon at Athens was hospitable even to his fellow members of the Laciad *curia* [ward]; for he had arranged it so, and had ordered his stewards, that everything should be provided for any Laciad who stopped at his country house.
passages.notes: 'curiales' is Cicero's Roman term for the members of Cimon's Athenian deme, Lakiadai.

passages.original: Ex quo genere comparationis illud est Catonis senis: a quo cum quaereretur, quid maxime in re familiari expediret, respondit: Bene pascere; quid secundum: Satis bene pascere; quid tertium: Male pascere; quid quartum: Arare; et cum ille, qui quaesierat, dixisset: Quid faenerari?, tum Cato: Quid hominem, inquit, occidere?
passages.english: Of this kind of comparison is that [saying] of Cato the Elder: when he was asked what was most profitable in managing an estate, he replied, "Grazing [cattle] well"; what second: "Grazing fairly well"; what third: "Grazing badly"; what fourth: "Ploughing"; and when the man who had asked him said, "What about lending at interest?", then Cato said, "What about killing a man?"

passages.original: P. Scipionem, M. fili, eum, qui primus Africanus appellatus est, dicere solitum scripsit Cato, qui fuit eius fere aequalis, numquam se minus otiosum esse, quam cum otiosus, nec minus solum, quam cum solus esset. Magnifica vero vox et magno viro ac sapiente digna; quae declarat illum et in otio de negotiis cogitare et in solitudine secum loqui solitum, ut neque cessaret umquam et interdum colloquio alterius non egeret.
passages.english: Cato, who was roughly his contemporary, wrote, Marcus my son, that Publius Scipio, the one who was first called Africanus, used to say that he was never less at leisure than when he was at leisure, nor less alone than when he was alone. A magnificent saying indeed, and worthy of a great and wise man; it shows that he was accustomed both to think about business in his leisure and to converse with himself in solitude, so that he was never idle and at times did not need conversation with another.

passages.original: Accedit eodem testis locuples Posidonius, qui etiam scribit in quadam epistula P. Rutilium Rufum dicere solere, qui Panaetium audierat, ut nemo pictor esset inventus, qui in Coa Venere eam partem, quam Apelles inchoatam reliquisset, absolveret (oris enim pulchritudo reliqui corporis imitandi spem auferebat), sic ea, quae Panaetius praetermisisset et non perfecisset propter eorum, quae perfecisset, praestantiam neminem persecutum.
passages.english: To the same [point] comes a substantial witness, Posidonius, who also writes in a certain letter that Publius Rutilius Rufus, who had heard Panaetius, used to say that, just as no painter had been found to complete that part of the Venus of Cos which Apelles had left begun (for the beauty of the face removed any hope of imitating the rest of the body), so no one had followed up those things which Panaetius had passed over and not completed, because of the excellence of those he had completed.

passages.original: Atque hoc loco philosoplis quidam, minime mali illi quidem, sed non satis acuti, fictam et commenticiam fabulam prolatam dicunt a Platone; quasi vero ille aut factum id esse aut fieri potuisse defendat! Ilaec est vis huius anuli et huius exempli: si nemo sciturus, nemo ne suspicaturus quidemn sit, cum aliquid divitiarum, potentiae, dominationis, libidinis causa feceris, si id dis hominibusque futurum sit semper ignotuml, sisne facturus.
passages.english: And at this point certain philosophers, not at all bad men indeed, but not sharp enough, say that a made-up and invented tale has been put forward by Plato; as if he were maintaining that it either happened or could have happened! This is the force of this ring and of this example: if no one were going to know, no one even to suspect, when you had done something for the sake of riches, power, domination or lust, if it were going to remain forever unknown to gods and men, would you do it?
passages.notes: Refers to the ring of Gyges (Plato, Republic). Scanning errors corrected: philosoplis, Ilaec, quidemn, ignotuml.

passages.original: Nec tamen nostrae nobis utilitates omittendae sunt aliisque tradendae, cum iis ipsi egeamus, sed suae cuique utilitati, quod sine alterius iniuria fiat, serviendum est. Scite Chrysippus, ut multa: Qui stadium, inquit, currit, eniti et contendere debet, quam maxime possit, ut vincat, supplantare eum, quicum certet, aut manu depellere nullo modo debet; sic in vita sibi quemque petere, quod pertineat ad usum, non iniquum est, alteri deripere ius non est.
passages.english: Yet we need not neglect our own interests and hand them over to others when we ourselves need them; rather each must serve his own interest, so far as it can be done without injury to another. Chrysippus put it cleverly, as he did many things: "He who runs a race," he said, "ought to strive and exert himself as much as he can to win; he ought by no means to trip his competitor or push him away with his hand. So in life it is not unjust for each to seek for himself what serves his needs, but it is not right to snatch it from another."

passages.original: Utile videbatur Ulixi, ut quidem poëtae tragici prodiderunt (nam apud Homerum, optimum auctorem, talis de Ulixe nulla suspicio est), sed insimulant eum tragoediae simulatione insaniae militiam subterfugere voluisse. Non honestum consilium, at utile, ut aliquis fortasse dixerit, regnare et Ithacae vivere otiose cum parentibus, cum uxore, cum filio.
passages.english: It seemed advantageous to Ulysses, as the tragic poets at least have related (for in Homer, the best authority, there is no such suspicion about Ulysses), but the tragedies accuse him of having wished to evade military service by feigning madness. Not an honourable plan, but an advantageous one, as someone might perhaps have said: to reign and to live at ease in Ithaca with his parents, his wife and his son.

passages.original: An ne turpiter faceret? Primum minima de malis. Num igitur tantum mali turpitude ista habebat, quantum ille cruciatus? Deinde illud etiam apud Accium: Fregistín fidem?Néque dedi neque do ínfideli cuíquam quamquam ab impio rege dicitur, luculente tamen dicitur.
passages.english: Or [was it] so as not to act shamefully? First, [choose] the least of evils. Did that shamefulness, then, carry as much evil as that torture? Next, there is also that passage in Accius: "Have you broken your faith?" "I neither have given nor give it to anyone faithless." Although it is said by an impious king, it is nevertheless said splendidly.

passages.original: est enim ius iurandum affirmatio religiosa; quod autem affirmate quasi deo teste promiseris, id tenendum est. Iam enim non ad iram deorum, quae nulla est, sed ad iustitiam et ad fidem pertinet. Nam praeclare Ennius: Ó Fides alma ápta pinnis ét ius iurandúm Iovis! Qui ius igitur iurandum violat, is Fidem violat, quam in Capitolio vicinam Iovis optimi maximi, ut in Catonis oratione est, maiores nostri esse voluerunt.
passages.english: For an oath is a solemn affirmation; and what you have promised affirmatively, as if with God as witness, must be kept. For it now concerns not the anger of the gods, which does not exist, but justice and good faith. For Ennius [says] admirably: "O kindly Faith, fitted with wings, and oath of Jupiter!" Whoever therefore violates an oath violates Faith, whom our ancestors wished to be on the Capitol as neighbour of Jupiter Best and Greatest, as is said in a speech of Cato.

passages.original: Non enim falsum iurare periurare est, sed, quod EX ANIMI TUI SENTENTIA iuraris, sicut verbis concipitur more nostro, id non facere periurium est. Scite enim Euripides: Iurávi lingua, méntem iniuratám gero. Regulus vero non debuit condiciones pactionesque bellicas et hostiles perturbare periurio. Cum iusto enim et legitimo hoste res gerebatur, adversus quem et totum ius fetiale et multa sunt iura communia.
passages.english: For to swear falsely is not [necessarily] perjury; but not to do what you have sworn "according to your conscience" (ex animi tui sententia), as it is formulated in words by our custom, that is perjury. For Euripides put it cleverly: "I swore with my tongue; I keep my mind unsworn." But Regulus ought not to have upset the terms and agreements of war and of enemies by perjury. For the matter was being conducted with a just and lawful enemy, towards whom both the whole fetial law and many rights held in common apply.

passages.original: Iam, qui dolorem summum malum dicat, apud eum quem habet locum fortitudo, quae est dolorum laborumque contemptio? Quamvis enim multis locis dicat Epicurus, sicuti dicit, satis fortiter de dolore, tamen non id spectandum est, quid dicat, sed quid consentaneum sit ei dicere, qui bona voluptate terminaverit, mala dolore.
passages.english: Next, for one who says that pain is the greatest evil, what place does courage have, which is the contempt of pains and toils? For although Epicurus speaks in many places, as he does, quite courageously about pain, still we must consider not what he says, but what is consistent for a man to say who has defined goods by pleasure and evils by pain.
